entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Titus Quinctius Flamininus, a scion of the Roman Republic's patrician gens Quinctia, emerged as a pivotal figure in the 2nd century BCE, instrumental in shifting the balance of power from the Hellenistic kingdoms to Rome. Born around 229 BCE, his military and diplomatic prowess culminated in the decisive defeat of Philip V of Macedon and the subsequent declaration of Greek 'freedom' in 196 BCE, effectively inaugurating Roman hegemony over the eastern Mediterranean. His career, marked by a consulship in 198 BCE at an unusually young age, fundamentally reshaped the geopolitical landscape of the Classical world, intertwining Roman ambition with Greek cultural influence.

Flamininus's most significant military triumph occurred at the Battle of Cynoscephalae in Thessaly in 197 BCE, where his legions, employing superior tactical flexibility, decisively crushed the Macedonian phalanx. This victory forced Philip V to accept a punitive peace treaty, relinquishing his control over Greece. The following year, at the Isthmian Games in Corinth, Flamininus dramatically proclaimed the freedom of all Greeks from Macedonian rule, a move met with ecstatic celebrations. While framed as liberation, this act was a shrewd diplomatic maneuver, replacing overt Macedonian dominance with a more subtle, yet equally firm, Roman influence, setting the stage for future interventions and eventual annexation.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Titus Quinctius Flamininus's actions fundamentally reshaped the geopolitical landscape of the eastern Mediterranean, dismantling the Hellenistic balance of power and establishing Roman hegemony over Greece. His 'liberation' effectively ended Greek independence and accelerated Rome's transformation into a dominant world power.
